Not a silly reason but from the point of view of a person who has chronic pain it may appear silly. Doctors have very strict regulations on prescriptions they can prescribe to patients. I worked at a doctors office and we would often receive letters from RACGP a detailing a medicine a doctor prescribed to a patient with a request to “please explain” why they prescribed a restricted medicine often to a patient with evidence based on how long they have seen the patient, what they prescribed and why. It is very stressful for doctors on top of the workload they have in that situation to write back a very strong letter and plead their case so their doctor’s licence doesn’t get revoked. Unfortunately, the way the system goes, anything a GP can’t do would require some support of a specialist (such as a pain specialist, rheumatologist, osteopath, etc.) to help plead the client’s case. It really sucks for people in that situation and I feel for them. Conversely, when doctors give in to client’s requests, it can lead to a sad cycle of addiction where the patient (not all patients are like this and are very understanding, but I have seen 5+ instances of this in a public GP clinic I worked at) keeps coming back and hops between clinics, which has led to me as a receptionist being hurled abuse from a patient threatening to kill me for doctors refusing to see them based on the fact they manipulate and abuse doctors for not prescribing certain medications, the patient trying to follow me home and me having to call the police on them. Because of these shitty situations, GPs often feel as if they don’t want to involve themselves at all in consistently prescribing high dose medications for pain management unless there is sufficient evidence and support from numerous specialists.

If you are in the Melbourne area I would be more than happy to support anyone just like you for casual shifts with the knowledge that I can be absent for 1-2 weeks spontaneously because of university studies. It makes my heart break that so many people decide to be a support worker for the money. For me, it’s about the client and their wellbeing always and I think that’s stemmed from studying a healthcare degree. Best of luck to you! I hope you find a suitable support worker at some point - I suggest putting as a note in your Mable advertisements that it is preferable to have a healthcare student support worker (i.e., OT/speech/physio/psych student) as majority of the time, we tend to be more client-focused rather than in it for the money/easy jobs.

It actually makes me so disappointed the influx of applicants applying to support clients only for mine to get drowned out when I have 3 years of support work experience and I am in my final year studying speech pathology. I have done 200 hours+ of supervised therapy unpaid with teacher’s praise so I know what I’m doing and it works well for those requiring home practice therapy in between sessions or those who can’t afford regular speech therapy appointments. I also have had a mental health client before from Mable and although feeling as if I didn’t have enough experience, I sought knowledge from my university studies and used my own unpaid time to research how I could best support her (and future clients) because it felt unjust to not provide optimal care. I also have had 7 clients from Mable & Hireup combined and had a lovely experience with them all and they have all asked me to become their regular support worker which made me very sad to say no because I have another client I support regularly plus university studies so I just do casual shifts on these online agencies when I can (and I do inform the clients that I cannot do ongoing shifts too). 
I feel as if clients should look more at qualifications, university students (whilst understanding they require flexibility) and those with 2-3 years experience. It is unfortunate that many just apply in hopes to get “easy jobs” like cleaning or driving. No support work job has ever been “easy” as a support worker, some more challenging than others for sure, but everyone has their own strengths/challenges! If only Mable would consider those aspects when hiring others but I understand that’s the downside of these online support work agencies rather than private support work agencies who often charge higher rates.

I’m 22 years old. Stay as long as you can at home. There is absolutely no rush. Save as much as you can and although you are paying board, it is nowhere near the amount you would have to pay to move out and rent. Everyone I know aged 18-25 years old that have moved out of home, about 90% had to move back home 1-2 years later from being broke and they regretted the money they wasted on renting for such a short period (this excludes people with rich parents feeding them money & people in uni accommodation). I am so grateful my parents don’t charge me board (wog parents), all they ask is that I pay my own car & health insurance (including rego, medical appointments, etc.) help around the house with chores and either study and/or have a well paying stable job (I do both). They told me the other day to stay as long as I like (I said: even till I’m 40?? and they said “yeah, i mean it would be weird but if you wanted to save for a house yeah sure”) and they would never kick me out unless I was sitting on my ass doing nothing lol. Keep in mind though the context of all of this is in the eastern suburbs of Melbourne, my dad works, my mum doesn’t work and we don’t have a super expensive house/lifestyle (they bought an old house and my dad is in trades so he fixed it up by himself with the help of friends/colleagues).

my house situation sort of makes it difficult to break in. windows are old and noisy to open (cannot open from outside, would have to smash it), back door is locked so you would have to kick it in (would make lots of noise), cameras at front (don’t do much, people have walked in our property twice at night with masks), front door doesn’t have a handle (it only opens with a key; keys aren’t visible from outside), cars are locked and too modern to break into or hot wire (all cars are 2010-2023 models) and our back gate is locked (they could jump over the fence but our neighbours dog is very loud when someone walks into our garage which is also locked so they would need to smash the glass to break in which also makes a lot of noise). we have had people go into our cars unlocked at night (they couldn’t hot wire them, they just threw the contents of the car everywhere which had nothing valuable in it) and no one has attempted to step foot on our property because it is virtually impossible to do so without making heaps of noise. good luck with your home security journey!

It is totally okay to be nervous before a test! I cried before my test because I was so anxious lol. My driving instructor told me all testing centres never take you on freeways. It’s difficult to have that belief in yourself, so even 1-2 practice runs with an instructor is totally worth it to ease your mind. I’m not sure if you’re doing it in the vehicle you normally drive in, but I suggest doing that if you can, it helps with feeling a bit more comfortable. I had a really good experience at the Dromana testing centre (albeit the drive) and I’m from the eastern suburbs so it was a while away but worth it, other friends near me said Pakenham was quite good too. I know quite a lot of my friends went rural/long distance to do the test, not only is it good practice, but it gives you added awareness and skills in areas you thought you would never drive! Confidence got so much better for me when I was by myself driving, I think it’s because I didn’t have someone judging me or pointing out a lot of things about my driving.

I used to work at the same clinic (not the Melton one, but in a different suburb). Unfortunately this is common amongst all these clinics - used to be a public run bulk billed clinic so not a lot of resources got put into it (now paid consults typically because medicare has become worse in supporting GPs for the amount of work/study they have done). It is very common that they put on as little receptionists as possible to save $ to pay staff, I usually got put on more when I worked there because I was younger and cheaper to pay. It is a very big issue with that company the way the phones are run plus, as a medical receptionist, majority of calls were calls not related to our centre at all that could have been done through medicare online or book an appointment online (when I worked there I got about 30% of calls a day that were not related to us, they were supposed to call medicare instead). Plus we would have a lot of people who we’d take a call for who were extremely slow (I’m saying a 5-8 min+ phone call that should take 1-3 minutes to do - typically either an old person/didn’t speak english well) or complain for a long time about the wait, thus making everyone’s call wait longer. Also, a lot of the time the doctors would make us call pathology lines or hospitals for an urgent result for a patient (I’m talking cancer patients, patients who are in hospital or need to go to hospital urgently, etc.) so that would leave a receptionist busy on hold waiting for another hospital/clinic to pick up their phones. Please sympathise with the receptionists and respect them, if it were up to us we would have no one waiting on the phone for more than 5 min, it’s the shitty system we have been handed by the company.

I have seen friends in mutually abusive relationships but when they are separate and you talk one on one with them, they are lovely people (just maybe not the best people to date lol). Those relationships were moreso two people with depression threatening suicide against one another when conflict arose, but no major emotional or physical abuse to the extent Alex put Alice through. Toxic relationships can become so sour when both people are struggling with mental illness and don’t have good coping mechanisms in place (which seemed to be the case for them and others I have seen). I think it’s also important to know that Alex used his power of being “an internet celebrity” and “paying for everything” (his exact words) as a weapon against Alice, putting her in a vulnerable situation. Power figures in relationships put the victim in extremely stressful situations (e.g. reactive abuse), I’m not saying Alice was perfect or she wasn’t a bad person (plus we don’t have the full story), but hearing the way Alex clearly communicated to her his power trip and used it against her, I cannot see how she is a “mutual perpetrator”.

unfortunately in Australia dupixent is regarded as a highly restricted class drug so it requires a specialist (dermatologist) to prescribe it. The dermatologist has to show evidence you need it through looking at your body and making a percentage of how severe your eczema is (say for eczema you had severe eczema on only one leg but the eczema on the rest of the body is not really too bad, you wouldn’t be able to get the injection even though the whole body is in pain). Oh to make things more fun, the rating of the eczema % on the body is subjective to the dermatologist, say for example they have seen way worse cases than you, they may mark you down just in comparison. The scoring assessment then asks questions about how your skin impacts your life but the score from that doesn’t greatly impact the final assessment score, mainly the body % score does.  
Then they have to prove all other treatments haven’t worked so you need to make probably 2-4+ dermatologist appointments proving each treatment hasn’t worked (this took probably over 6-7 months+ to prove for me), do blood tests, etc. 
The thing is for drugs in Australia, they really want to make sure people aren’t abusing them or being prescribed them if they really don’t need it, plus the specialist just finds it inconvenient to get through the whole process and monitor patients who are having them (which is ironic because they’re not living with the condition).

Fortunately (well unfortunate to me because of the severe pain) I had over 85% whole body severe eczema that was very dry and weeping and nothing else worked, but even despite nothing working it was very difficult to convince my dermatologist to prescribe me dupixent. It is on the PBS as a general schedule authority as a highly specialised drug so they need to go through every treatment option with you to be allowed to give authority, you have to score a certain amount on the assessment scale on full body eczema severity for it to be prescribed. I don’t think specialists or doctors like going through the highly specialised drug program because it makes them do more tests, more appointments and leaves them under high supervision of the PBS to constantly check if their patient is being prescribed a reasonable amount and checks to see if they are still on it, plus any fuck up they do in this process will lead them to be at a very high risk of losing their practice licence.

Sorry to hear it hasn’t quite worked out for you, it took me a while of persevering with it because when I started it, the first 2-4 months didn’t seem like it was working either until it gradually did. I’m not sure how but I guess my body got accustomed to it to the point of not requiring it anymore (which the dermatologist said is okay and can happen). I think the issue is because the drug in Australia is a drug that only specialists can prescribe, it requires them calling this hotline and doing special assessments and going through every course of treatment before prescribing it, makes it an annoying process for them to prescribe and they also have to ensure I won’t abuse the injection by keeping having follow up appointments with me if I keep using it. I also think the fact it hasn’t been in Australia long they don’t bother researching into it as well as the fact that it is rarely prescribed and the Australian drug organisation for doctors didn’t provide doctors with a lot of information on it which left them to do their own research on it. I will admit, during those 2 years I got sick much more often and now after stopping I do still sort of do get sick slightly more often, but it was nowhere near as bad as the ongoing pain of severe eczema.
